Stage 2 · Results · Simulated test world: 579 wells, two datasets

Half the error of reading the gauge, and a clear view of what is still missing.

Every number is on the test year, August 2025 to July 2026: a forecast issued every Sunday for every well from data up to that day, scored once against the simulated true weekly level. How the model works.

Error now (nowcast), dataset A0.52 m0.91 m for the latest rested reading
4 weeks ahead0.61 m1.05 m holding the reading flat
12 weeks ahead0.74 m1.48 m flat; 1.15 m seasonal guess
Dataset B, 12 weeks ahead0.70 m1.56 m flat; settings frozen from A

Error by weeks ahead

The model starts at half the error of the gauge and stays there: its error grows by about 0.2 m over twelve weeks, the gauge's by about 0.6 m.

What we said we expected, before running it

Four expectations were written into the plan and fingerprinted before any model ran. Three held on dataset A; one held on dataset B.

Expected in advanceDataset ADataset B
Beats holding the reading flat, at every horizonMet: 43–50 % less errorMet: 51–55 % less error
Terrain-based start cuts the 12-week error on never-fitted wells by at least 10 %Met, just: 1.13 → 1.01 m (−11 %)Missed: 1.02 → 0.94 m (−8 %)
Sensor layer cuts the nowcast error on faulty-sensor wells by at least halfMet: 2.68 → 1.11 m (−59 %)Missed: 3.40 → 1.97 m (−42 %)

What each part is worth

Average error, metres (lower is better)

The sensor-fault layer matters most where sensors fail; the reading-time layer matters most on slow-recovering wells; the water physics matters most beyond a month, where holding even a cleaned reading flat falls behind.

By type of well

The simulator gives every well a hidden type from its terrain. The model never sees it; it is used here only to break down the scores.

"Reads too deep" is the model's average nowcast minus the true level: a positive number means the model places the water table deeper than it is.

What did not work: the slow wells

Ridge wells in fractured rock and low-yield wells are still read about 1 m too deep (the gauge: about 1.8 m). The reason is in the data, not the model.

A fast valley well

Recovers within hours: by the next session the reading is back at the true level.

A slow ridge well

Never recovers between sessions: every reading carries the same standing drawdown.

Water level in the well True water table (what we forecast) Reading at the start of a session

Illustration, not data: two sessions a day at 06:00 and 18:00. When a well always pumps on the same schedule, its standing drawdown is the same in every reading, and from level readings alone it cannot be told apart from a deeper water table. Fitted recovery times came out negatively related to the true ones (rank correlation −0.39 on A, −0.31 on B): the evidence simply is not in the readings.

The fix is a field practice, not more modelling

A 48-hour pump-off rest once a month on slow wells, or a logger that keeps recording while the pump is off, would show how far each well recovers, and give an unbiased check for the ranges below.

Are the ranges honest? Not yet.

The "80 % likely" range holds 3 % of the time for the nowcast and 63–67 % at twelve weeks. It is too narrow, mostly on the slow wells.

Dataset A Dataset B Target: 80 %

Share of weeks where the true level fell inside the 80 % range

Why: the ranges were set on the previous year against the model's own smoothed history, because the plan allows only data-side targets. That history carries the same slow-well bias, so the ranges are confidently narrow exactly where the model is wrong. By type at 12 weeks (A): valley wells 68–76 %, ridge weathered 67 %, ridge fractured 48 %, low yield 42 %. Unbiased long-rest readings from the field would fix the calibration.

What this shows
  • Separating the true level from the reading halves the error of reading the gauge, now and twelve weeks ahead, on two differently built datasets.
  • The pump is a usable second depth gauge: it finds 80–88 % of faulty sensors with few false alarms. Sensor faults →
  • Terrain from public-quality maps helps most for wells with no history, at longer horizons. Terrain →
What is not proven
  • Everything is on simulated wells we built; the model's water balance is from the same family as the simulator's, so field results will be lower.
  • Slow wells stay biased and the ranges are too narrow until the field provides long-rest readings.
  • The reading-time correction slightly hurts the fastest valley wells (0.18 m against 0.09 m without it).

See individual wells →

Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
